Key Research Thinking Patterns: Deep Learning for Inverse Force Reconstruction: Utilizing transfer learning with pre-trained CNNs (VGG19, InceptionResNetV2) on synthetic photoelastic data to accurately infer inter-particle forces from experimental images, bypassing the computational cost of traditional optimization methods.

Topological Data Analysis for Slip Precursor Identification: Applying persistent homology to force network persistence diagrams derived from G2 strain data to detect nontrivial structural changes and topological fluctuations that serve as early warning signals for impending slip events.

Multi-Scale Statistical Monitoring of Granular Instability: Comparing global system-wide averages against local micro/mesoscale metrics (Wasserstein distance, broken contact counts) to reveal that local fluctuations, rather than global averages, are sensitive indicators of approaching stick-slip transitions.

Computational Conley Theory for Global Dynamics: Integrating neural networks with Conley index theory to learn phase space discretizations from orbit data, enabling the robust identification of attracting neighborhoods and correct computation of Conley indices for complex dynamical attractors.
Summary Description: Miroslav Kramar specializes in the intersection of soft matter physics, granular mechanics, and advanced computational methods. His research focuses on characterizing the statics and dynamics of granular materials, particularly stick-slip phenomena relevant to geological hazards and industrial processing. He employs a hybrid methodology combining experimental photoelasticity with machine learning and topological data analysis. Key contributions include developing CNN-based inverse models for efficient force reconstruction and utilizing persistent homology to identify topological precursors to slip events. Additionally, he integrates Conley index theory with neural networks to robustly characterize global dynamical systems. His work bridges experimental mechanics with data-driven science to predict instability in complex, non-linear systems.
